How Long Does NDT Training Take? Level I, II & III Timelines Explained

Real classroom-hour and on-the-job experience-hour timelines for NDT Level I, II, and III certification, and why OJT hours — not classroom time — are what actually gate your progress.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · August 8, 2026

How Long Does NDT Training Take?

Classroom training for NDT Level I typically runs around 40 hours (about one week full-time), Level II around 80 hours, and Level III 120+ hours per method. But classroom time is only part of the picture — SNT-TC-1A also requires documented on-the-job experience hours before you can sit each level's exam, which is what actually stretches total time-to-certified from days into months or years.

Classroom Hours by Level

Atlantis NDT's own Level I, II, and III courses run 40, 80, and 120 hours respectively — see the exact course structure on our training programs page. Those figures track closely with the broader industry norm, though the SNT-TC-1A recommended practice actually specifies classroom hours per method, and they vary: some methods (like Visual Testing) require fewer hours than others (like Ultrasonic or Radiographic Testing) because the underlying physics and equipment are simpler. The Part Everyone Underestimates: On-the-Job Experience Hours

Here's the honest answer to "how long is NDT training" that a lot of shorter guides skip: classroom hours are not the bottleneck. You can finish a Level I classroom course in a single week. What actually determines when you're eligible to sit for your next certification exam is your accumulated, documented on-the-job experience hours — logged under the supervision of a certified Level II or III, per your employer's written practice.

Under SNT-TC-1A, the general experience-hour framework looks roughly like this (exact figures vary by method and by your employer's written practice):

  • Level I: around 300 hours of documented OJT, which most full-time trainees accumulate in about 3 months
  • Level II: either roughly 2,400 additional OJT hours, or Level I certification plus about one additional year of documented experience — whichever path your employer's written practice specifies
  • Level III: a minimum of about 10,000 hours of total NDT work (roughly 5 years), plus Level II certification in at least three methods and 150+ hours of formal Level III training

Put together, that means: Level I is realistically a 3 to 4 month proposition for a full-time trainee. Level II, where most independent field inspectors sit, realistically takes 1 to 2 years from a standing start. Level III is a 5 to 7 year proposition minimum, and in practice often longer, because it also requires you to be certified Level II in multiple methods before you're eligible.

Realistic Total Timeline: Classroom Start to Working Level II Inspector

MilestoneRealistic timeframe from a standing start
Complete Level I classroom course1 to 2 weeks
Accumulate Level I OJT hours + pass Level I exam+2 to 3 months
Working as certified Level I, accumulating Level II OJT hours+9 to 18 months
Complete Level II classroom course + pass Level II exam+1 to 4 weeks (can overlap with OJT accumulation)
Total: entry to working, independent Level II inspector~1 to 2 years

Two things shorten this in practice. First, many employers run training and OJT in parallel — you're logging hours on real work while your classroom certification is in progress, rather than doing them sequentially. Second, if you already work in an adjacent trade (welding, machining, quality inspection) some of your prior technical exposure can shorten the ramp-up, even though it doesn't substitute for the documented NDT-specific experience hours themselves.

Why This Matters When Choosing a Training Program

Because OJT hours — not classroom seat time — are the real bottleneck, the single most useful thing a training provider or employer can offer isn't a shorter course; it's a clear, realistic pathway to accumulating supervised experience hours afterward. When evaluating any NDT training program, ask directly: who is going to sign off on my OJT hours, and how long does that typically take at this company? A 40-hour classroom certificate that leads nowhere for OJT placement doesn't actually get you to Level II any faster than a slower classroom course with a strong placement pipeline behind it.

What Actually Speeds Up or Slows Down Your Timeline

The 1-to-2-year Level II timeline above is a realistic midpoint, not a fixed rule. A handful of factors move it meaningfully in either direction:

  • Full-time vs. part-time exposure: OJT hours accumulate based on documented time actually performing the method, not calendar time. A trainee working NDT full-time will clear the 2,400-hour Level II threshold far faster than someone doing it part-time or intermittently alongside other duties.
  • Employer sign-off capacity: Your hours only count once a certified Level II or III reviews and documents them. A company with several available Level IIIs and an established written practice can turn around sign-offs quickly; a smaller shop with one overstretched Level III can create bottlenecks that have nothing to do with your actual skill level.
  • Which method you choose first: Visual Testing and Liquid Penetrant Testing carry lower classroom-hour requirements than Ultrasonic or Radiographic Testing, so a first certification in VT or PT is simply faster to reach than a first certification in UT or RT, independent of how hard you study.
  • Prior adjacent experience: Time spent in welding, machining, or quality inspection doesn't substitute for NDT-specific OJT hours, but it does shorten the practical learning curve during classroom training and early fieldwork, which can indirectly speed up how quickly you're trusted with more hours.
  • Multi-method certification: Adding a second or third method after your first Level II is usually faster than the first one was, since classroom fundamentals overlap and you're already established with an employer who can document your hours.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: How long does NDT training take overall, start to Level II?

A: Realistically 1 to 2 years from a standing start with no prior NDT experience — a few months to reach Level I, then 9 to 18 months of documented on-the-job experience hours before you're eligible to sit the Level II exam.

Q2: How long is NDT training for just the classroom portion?

A: Around 40 hours (about one week) for a typical Level I course, roughly 80 hours for Level II, and 120+ hours for Level III — though exact hours vary by method under SNT-TC-1A.

Q3: Can I speed up the on-the-job experience-hour requirement?

A: Not by skipping it — SNT-TC-1A requires documented, supervised hours regardless of how fast you learn the material. You can shorten the calendar time by working full-time in a role that generates qualifying hours quickly, rather than part-time or intermittently.

Q4: Does NDT training take longer for some methods than others?

A: Yes. Visual Testing and Liquid Penetrant Testing generally require fewer classroom hours than Ultrasonic or Radiographic Testing, reflecting the relative complexity of the equipment and physics involved.

Q5: How long does it take to reach NDT Level III?

A: A minimum of roughly 5 to 7 years, requiring about 10,000 hours of total documented NDT experience, Level II certification in at least three methods, and passing ASNT's Basic and Method exams.
